title: Can you edit a human being's DNA?
subtitle: The CRISPR scissors
subject: sciences
description: Since 2012, "molecular scissors" borrowed from bacteria have made it possible to cut DNA exactly where we want. First cures, possible mistakes and designer babies: how far will it go?
author: kate-waddams

hero.hook: What if you could fix a letter in your DNA the way you fix a typo?

blocks.text: Hair, eyes, skin color, body shape: we all look different. These physical traits come down to inheritance: each [[gene]] is a segment of DNA received from our biological parents. Our surroundings matter too: what we eat, the people around us, what we believe. But we take our genes for granted. We might wish we were taller or thinner, but we live with them without a second thought.

What would you change if you could edit your DNA? The question is no longer theoretical. In **2012**, an American biochemist, **Jennifer Doudna**, and a French microbiologist, **Emmanuelle Charpentier**, developed a way to program a protein that cuts DNA. From then on, they could remove an unwanted gene and so, in theory, edit the DNA of a human being.

[[CRISPR]] is not the only tool that can alter DNA, but it is the most famous. Its principle was first observed in microbes. To defend itself, a bacterium spots the DNA of the virus attacking it and chops it to pieces. To do so, it uses DNA segments called CRISPRs and an enzyme called **Cas**, which acts as the scissors.

blocks.caption: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna, the two researchers who turned this bacterial defense into a tool.

blocks.text: Scientists hijacked this natural defense system. Instead of aiming at a virus, they guide the enzyme to a precise spot on a person's DNA. There it cuts, and a deliberate change becomes possible. Sometimes the target gene is simply switched off. Sometimes a few of its letters are changed. Sometimes it is replaced entirely.

sections.title: The first cures: sickle cell disease and thalassemia

blocks.text: Being able to edit DNA opens the door to treating many genetic diseases. Our DNA is written with **four bases**, A, T, C and G. Their sequence forms our [[genome]], the building plan of our body. A single error in that text can be enough to trigger a disease, and correcting it can, in principle, cure it.

blocks.caption: Liver tissue from a sickle cell patient, seen under the microscope: the first illness treated with CRISPR.

blocks.text: In **2023**, the United Kingdom became the first country to approve a CRISPR-based medicine. It targets two inherited blood disorders, [[sickle cell disease]] and beta-thalassemia. The treatment edits the cells that make blood so that they produce more [[fetal hemoglobin]], a form of hemoglobin normally made before birth.
A typo can kill. A single wrong letter in the DNA, a T in place of a C for example, is sometimes enough to cause a fatal genetic disease. Putting the right letter back could, in theory, cure it.

And this is only the beginning. Clinical trials are now testing CRISPR against cancers, metabolic disorders, autoimmune diseases, cardiovascular disease and muscular dystrophy, among many others. The list is long. So will genetic diseases soon be a thing of the past?

sections.title: Why we will not cure everything

blocks.text: It is not that simple. First, how a gene is expressed does not depend only on what we inherit from our parents: the environment influences it too. Second, a disorder is not necessarily the work of a single faulty gene. Several genes can be involved, and repairing them becomes far more complicated.

CRISPR itself can make mistakes. Sometimes the scissors cut the wrong section of DNA, or the two cut ends fail to repair themselves properly. That altered DNA can create new problems without fixing the original one. Even so, medicine is taking big steps toward wiping out some of the worst genetic diseases.

sections.title: Designer babies: where do we draw the line?

blocks.text: Everyone can see the point of treating crippling or fatal diseases. But where should science draw the line? Should it be used to create the "perfect human"? The question has taken on new urgency now that DNA can be cut at will.

blocks.caption: A human egg cell held by a pipette during a micro-injection in the laboratory.

blocks.text: The phrase "designer baby" was not born with CRISPR. It has been in use since the arrival of [[in vitro fertilization]], which makes it possible to conceive an embryo in the laboratory before implanting it.

The technique known as [[germline editing]] alters the DNA of reproductive cells: sperm, eggs or embryos at their earliest stages. Unlike an ordinary treatment, those changes are then passed down from generation to generation. Today, germline editing is banned in every country. But for how long? At what point will medical gene editing make the leap to genetic lines on demand?

Since 2012, the CRISPR scissors have made it possible to correct human DNA, with the first cures approved in 2023, but mistakes remain possible, many diseases involve several genes, and germline editing stays banned everywhere.
